Difference: Ryegrass forms a dense, fine-textured lawn with narrow upright blades and produces high amounts of airborne pollen. Lily Turf (Liriope) grows in tidy clumps with broader, arching leaves and small purple flowers, and releases very little airborne pollen, making it safer for allergy-sensitive people.
Mainly found in: Gardens, shaded borders, landscaping areas in Victoria; commonly used as low-maintenance ground cover.

Difference: Plane Trees have broad, maple-like leaves, rough patchy bark, and produce round, spiky seed balls. Trident Maples have smaller, more delicate three-lobed leaves, smooth gray bark, and produce winged seeds (samaras) in clusters, making them easier to distinguish.
Mainly found in: Urban gardens, streetscapes, and parks across Victoria.

Difference: Silver Birch has small, triangular serrated leaves, smooth white bark that peels in thin sheets, and produces long catkins releasing large amounts of fine airborne pollen. Paperbark Trees have narrow, elongated leaves, rough pale bark that flakes in thick layers, and produce creamy bottlebrush-like flowers with very low airborne pollen.
Mainly found in: Streets, parks, wetlands, and gardens throughout Victoria.

Difference: Bermuda Grass forms a dense lawn with fine, wiry leaves and produces large amounts of airborne pollen during flowering. Sir Walter Buffalo Grass has broader, flatter, and softer leaves, grows by thick runners, flowers much less frequently, and releases minimal airborne pollen, making it a safer choice for allergy-sensitive lawns.
Mainly found in: Home lawns, parks, schools, and shaded gardens across Victoria.

Difference: Timothy Grass grows upright with fine leaves and tall cylindrical flower spikes that release large amounts of airborne pollen. Lomandra forms dense clumps with long, strap-like leaves and small, hidden flowers that produce minimal airborne pollen, making it much safer for allergy-sensitive landscapes.
Mainly found in: Public parks, roadside plantings, gardens across Victoria.

Difference: Mulberry trees have broad, textured leaves that may be lobed or unlobed, with rough bark and edible fruits, and produce moderate amounts of airborne pollen. Small-leaved Lime Trees have heart-shaped, smooth-edged leaves and small fragrant flowers, releasing lower levels of airborne pollen, making them a milder alternative for allergy-sensitive areas.
Mainly found in: Streetscapes, parks, and public gardens across Victoria.

Difference: Olive Trees have leathery, grey-green narrow leaves, rough bark, and produce small green fruits along with heavy airborne pollen. Mayten Trees have finer, soft green leaves arranged on graceful weeping branches and produce minimal airborne pollen, making them a gentler alternative for allergy-sensitive gardens.
Mainly found in: seen in botanical gardens, private gardens, and arboretums.

Difference: Atlas Cedar has thick, bluish-green needles arranged in dense clusters on sturdy horizontal branches and produces upright barrel-shaped cones. Engelmann Spruce has softer, shorter bluish needles arranged radially around the twig and produces hanging, slender cones, with a more conical overall tree shape.
Mainly found in: Rarely planted in Victoria; mainly found in specialized gardens and cooler mountain areas.

Difference: Elm Trees have rough, deeply furrowed bark, asymmetrical toothed leaves, and release large amounts of airborne pollen. Japanese Zelkova has smoother, grayish bark, more symmetrical finely toothed leaves, and produces much less airborne pollen, making it a safer alternative for allergy-sensitive landscapes.
Mainly found in: Streetscapes, parks, and gardens in Victoria, especially used as an Elm replacement.

Difference: Oak Trees have broad, lobed leaves with deep rounded edges and produce acorns as fruit, along with heavy airborne pollen. Sweetgum Trees have star-shaped leaves with pointed lobes and produce spiky round seed balls, while releasing less airborne pollen compared to Oaks.
Mainly found in: Public parks, gardens, and urban streetscapes across Victoria.

Difference: Pigweed grows upright with coarse, rough leaves and tall flowering spikes that release heavy airborne pollen. Chinese Spinach (Amaranthus tricolor) has softer, more tender leaves, shorter flowering spikes, and produces much less airborne pollen, making it a safer choice for allergy-sensitive gardens.
Mainly found in: Home vegetable gardens, farms, and some community gardens across Victoria.

Difference: Ragweed grows with coarse, rough, deeply lobed leaves and produces large amounts of airborne pollen. Sweet Cicely has delicate, finely divided fern-like leaves and small white flowers, producing very little airborne pollen, making it much safer for allergy-sensitive people.
Mainly found in: Gardens, herb beds, and shaded areas in Victoria.

Difference: Privet has small, smooth, oval leaves, dense white flower clusters, and produces heavy airborne pollen and small black berries. Lychee Trees have larger, glossy compound leaves, looser flower clusters, and produce edible fruits, with very low airborne pollen, making them much safer for allergy-sensitive gardens.
Mainly found in: In Victoria mainly found in private gardens.

Difference: Cocksfoot has coarse, upright blades with a clumping growth habit and a large, open flowering head. Woolly Poa is finer-textured with soft, narrow leaves and a woolly base; it grows in smaller, denser clumps and lacks the prominent seed heads of Cocksfoot.
Mainly found in: Native grasslands, dry forests, and landscaping in Victoria; used in eco-friendly planting

Difference: Paspalum urvillei is a tall, coarse, wind-pollinated grass with broad rough leaves and dense seed heads, known to trigger allergies. Urochloa lachnantha is shorter, softer, and more mat-forming with less airborne pollen, making it safer for allergy-sensitive individuals.
Mainly found in: In Victoria mainly found in private gardens and parks.
